title: Al-Jazari: Inventor of Machines
summary: The life and work of Al-Jazari, an engineer who built water pumps, an elephant clock, and moving automata about 800 years ago and wrote a famous book of machines.
poll: Inventors from long ago still shape the machines we use today.

versions.title: Al-Jazari Made Machines
versions.text:
Long ago, a man made smart machines. His name was Al-Jazari. He was an inventor.

He lived about 800 years ago. His home was by a big river. A king gave him work. He made things for the king.

He made a machine to lift water. It was a pump. It sent water up to farms. Then men did not have to lift it by hand.

He made a clock, too. It looked like a big elephant! Water made it work. Each half hour, a ball fell. A bird sang. That told the time.

He used gears. A gear is a wheel with teeth. When one gear turns, it turns the next one.

He made toys that moved on their own. One was a boat with a band. The band played a tune.

He wrote a book. He drew each machine. He told how to build it. We can still read it now.

Ideas like his are still used in machines now. He was a great inventor.

About 800 years ago, a man built some of the most clever machines of his time. His name was Al-Jazari, and he was a brilliant inventor.

Al-Jazari lived near the Tigris River. Today, that land is part of Turkey. A royal family hired him, and he worked for them for about twenty-five years. He built many amazing things.

One of his main goals was to lift water. He made a kind of pump that pushed water up from a river to fields and homes. Because of machines like this, people no longer had to carry heavy buckets by hand.

He also made clocks. His most famous one looked like a giant elephant! Water inside the elephant made the clock work. Every half hour, a ball dropped and a bird sang. A little figure moved, too. These signs told people the time.

Al-Jazari wrote a book about fifty of his machines. He drew careful pictures of each one. He also explained how to build it, so others could copy his work.

Ideas like his are still used in machines today. That is why Al-Jazari is remembered as a great inventor.

versions.title: Al-Jazari: Inventor of Machines
versions.text:
About 800 years ago, an engineer named Al-Jazari built some of the most clever machines of his time. Many of his ideas were far ahead of the world around him.

Al-Jazari lived near the Tigris River, in a region that is now part of Turkey. A royal family hired him, and he served them for about twenty-five years. His job was to design and build useful and surprising machines.

One of his main goals was to raise water. He built pumps that lifted water from a river to fields and homes. Some of his pumps were turned by animals, and others by flowing water. Because of these machines, farmers no longer had to carry heavy buckets by hand.

He also built clocks. His most famous one was shaped like a giant elephant. Inside, a bowl slowly sank in a tank of water. Every half hour, a ball dropped. A bird whistled, and a small figure moved. These signals told people the time.

Al-Jazari used gears, which are wheels with teeth that turn each other. He also used valves, which open and close to control how water flows.

He also created an automaton, a machine that moves by itself. One was a boat with four musicians. It floated on a pool and played music for guests.

In 1206, Al-Jazari finished a book that described fifty of his machines. For each device, he drew careful pictures and explained how to build it, so others could copy his work.

Ideas like his are still used in machines today. That is why Al-Jazari is remembered as a great inventor.

versions.title: Al-Jazari: Master of Ingenious Machines
versions.text:
About 800 years ago, an engineer named Al-Jazari constructed some of the most remarkable machines of his era, and many of his ideas were far ahead of the world around him.

Al-Jazari lived near the Tigris River, in a region that is now part of Turkey. A royal family employed him for approximately twenty-five years, and his responsibility was to design and construct machines that were both practical and astonishing.

One of his principal objectives was to raise water. He constructed pumps that lifted water from rivers to agricultural fields and homes, some powered by animals and others by flowing water. In one design, he connected a turning wheel to a crank, a bent arm that changes circular motion into a back-and-forth push, so that pistons could pump water steadily. Because of such inventions, farmers no longer needed to carry heavy buckets by hand.

He also built clocks, and his most celebrated one was shaped like a gigantic elephant. Inside it, a bowl gradually sank in a tank of water, and every half hour a ball dropped, a bird whistled, and a small figure moved. The clock combined ideas from several cultures, including an Indian elephant and Chinese-style dragons.

Al-Jazari used gears, which are toothed wheels that turn one another, and valves, which open and close to regulate the flow of water, so his machines could repeat their movements automatically.

Additionally, he created an automaton, a machine that operates independently. One was a boat carrying four mechanical musicians that floated on a pool and performed for guests. Its drummer was programmable, because pegs on a rotating drum could be moved to change the rhythm.

In 1206, Al-Jazari completed a manuscript known as The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices, which described fifty of his machines. For each device, he produced detailed illustrations and explained how to build it, so that others could reproduce his work.

His legacy endures today, since engineers still study his designs and ideas similar to his appear in modern machines. That is why Al-Jazari is remembered as an outstanding inventor.

versions.title: Al-Jazari: Master of Ingenious Machines
versions.text:
Approximately 800 years ago, an engineer named Al-Jazari constructed some of the most sophisticated machines of his era, and many of his ideas were considerably ahead of the technology of the world around him.

Al-Jazari lived near the Tigris River, in a region that now belongs to Turkey, where a royal dynasty employed him for approximately twenty-five years. His responsibility was to design and construct machines that were simultaneously practical and astonishing.

One of his principal objectives was to raise water, so he engineered pumps that lifted water from rivers to agricultural fields and households, some powered by animals and others by flowing water. In one design, he connected a rotating wheel to a crank, a bent arm that converts circular motion into a reciprocating push, so that pistons could pump water continuously. Historians consider this arrangement one of the earliest documented examples of a crank linked to a connecting rod within a working machine. Because of such inventions, farmers no longer needed to transport heavy buckets by hand.

He also built clocks, and his most celebrated one was shaped like a gigantic elephant. Inside it, a bowl gradually sank in a reservoir of water, and every half hour a ball dropped, a bird whistled, and a small figure moved. The clock deliberately combined ideas from several cultures, including an Indian elephant and Chinese-style dragons, reflecting the exchange of knowledge across distant civilizations.

Al-Jazari incorporated gears, which are toothed wheels that turn one another, and valves, which open and close to regulate the flow of water, so that his machines could repeat their movements automatically.

Additionally, he created an automaton, a machine that operates independently, and one remarkable example was a boat carrying four mechanical musicians that floated on a pool and performed for distinguished guests, and its drummer was programmable, because pegs on a rotating cylinder could be rearranged to alter the rhythm.

In 1206, Al-Jazari completed a manuscript known as The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices, which documented fifty of his machines. For each device, he produced meticulous illustrations and explained the construction process, so that subsequent engineers could reproduce his work.

His legacy endures today, since historians and engineers continue to analyze his designs and comparable mechanisms appear in contemporary machinery. Consequently, Al-Jazari is remembered as an extraordinary inventor whose creativity influenced generations of builders.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to tell time without a clock
An inventor from long ago and the machines he made
Why elephants like water
How to play music on a boat
questions.why: The whole article tells about Al-Jazari and the pumps, clocks, and moving toys he built.

wrong.A: The article is about machines, including a clock, not about telling time without one.
wrong.C: The elephant is the shape of a clock, not a real animal.
wrong.D: The music boat is only one of his machines.

questions.stem: What did Al-Jazari's pump do?
options: It made music for the king.
It showed the time each half hour.
It lifted water up to fields and homes.
It made the boat float.
questions.why: The article says his pump lifted water up to farms, fields, and homes.

wrong.A: The music came from the band on the boat.
wrong.B: The clock showed the time, not the pump.
wrong.D: The article does not say a pump made the boat float.

questions.stem: What was Al-Jazari's famous clock shaped like?

A big elephant
A bird

wrong.A: The article does not mention a tower.
wrong.B: The boat was a musical toy, not the clock.
wrong.D: A bird sang on the clock, but the clock was shaped like an elephant.

questions.stem: The article says a gear is a wheel with teeth. What happens when one gear turns?
options: It stops all the other wheels.
It makes water hot.
It lifts a ball into the air.
It turns the next gear.
questions.why: The article explains that when one gear turns, its teeth make the next gear turn.

wrong.A: Gears pass motion on; they do not stop it.
wrong.C: The ball dropping is part of the clock, not the meaning of gear.

questions.stem: What happened because of Al-Jazari's water pump?
options: People had to carry more water.
Rivers dried up.
The king stopped giving him work.
People did not have to lift water by hand.

wrong.B: The article does not say rivers dried up.
wrong.C: The article says he worked for the royal family; it does not say they stopped.

questions.stem: Why did Al-Jazari draw pictures and tell how to build each machine in his book?

So no one could copy his work
Because he could not write words
To sell the book to children
questions.why: The article says he drew and explained each machine so others could copy or build it, and we can still read it today.

wrong.B: He explained how to build them, which helps others copy them.
wrong.C: He wrote a book, so he could write.
wrong.D: The article does not say he sold the book.

questions.stem: Why do we still remember Al-Jazari today?
options: He was the king of a big land.
His ideas are still used in machines.
He had the biggest elephant.
He lived for a thousand years.
questions.why: The article ends by saying that ideas like his are still used in machines now, so he is remembered as a great inventor.

wrong.A: He worked for a royal family; he was not the king.
wrong.C: The elephant was a clock, not a real elephant he owned.
wrong.D: He lived about 800 years ago, but not for a thousand years.

questions.stem: How does the author organize most of the article?

By comparing Al-Jazari with a modern inventor
By telling one of his machines in each part

questions.stem: What does the mix of an Indian elephant and Chinese-style dragons in the clock suggest?
options: Al-Jazari had never traveled outside his own small town.
Ideas were shared among different cultures.
Clocks were only made in India.
Dragons were real animals then.
questions.why: The article says the clock combined ideas from several cultures, showing that knowledge was exchanged across civilizations.

wrong.A: The article says nothing about his travels.
wrong.C: The article does not say this.
wrong.D: The dragons were decorations, not real animals.

questions.stem: How did Al-Jazari's use of valves and gears affect his machines?
options: They stopped water from flowing at all.
They made the machines much heavier, slower, and harder to use.
They let the machines repeat their movements automatically.
They allowed the machines to run on electricity.
questions.why: The article says gears and valves let his machines repeat their movements automatically.

wrong.A: Valves control the flow; they do not stop it completely.
wrong.B: The article does not say this.
wrong.D: Electricity did not exist in his machines.

questions.stem: Which detail best supports the claim that Al-Jazari wanted others to learn from his work?
options: He worked for a royal family for about twenty-five years near the Tigris River.
His clock was shaped like a gigantic elephant.
He explained how to build each device with detailed illustrations.
His boat floated on a pool.
questions.why: Explaining construction with illustrations shows he wanted others to reproduce his machines.

wrong.A: This shows his job, not his wish to teach.
wrong.B: This describes a design, not teaching.
wrong.D: This describes an automaton, not teaching.

questions.stem: How is the water pump different from the musical boat in purpose?
options: The pump was built to entertain guests, while the boat was built to help farmers water fields.
The pump solved a practical problem, while the boat mainly entertained guests.
Both were built only to tell time.
Neither one used any moving parts.
questions.why: The pump lifted water for fields and homes, a practical need; the boat performed music for guests.

wrong.A: This reverses their purposes.

questions.stem: Why does the author end with Al-Jazari's legacy?
options: To list every machine in his book
To describe how he built the elephant clock
To argue that modern machines are worse
To explain why his work still matters to engineers today
questions.why: The ending links his 800-year-old work to engineers and machines today, showing why he is still remembered.

wrong.A: The ending does not list his fifty machines.
wrong.B: The clock is described in an earlier paragraph.
wrong.C: The author does not criticize modern machines.

HIGH.prompt: Some people call Al-Jazari one of the most important engineers in history. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that Al-Jazari was one of the most important engineers in history, because his inventions were remarkably ingenious for his time. He designed water pumps powered by animals and flowing water that let farmers stop hauling buckets by hand, and he built an elephant clock whose crank mechanism used falling balls, whistling birds, and moving figures to mark every half hour. Perhaps most impressively, his book described fifty machines in such careful, almost programmable detail that people could recreate his inventions centuries later from the surviving manuscript. Because his ideas still influence machines today, his legacy as an engineer is well deserved.
